stem: David is a 2-year-old boy with asthma that is well controlled on fluticasone and salbutamol. His mother asks whether the ‘asthma pill’ her nephew takes could be an option for him. In children, for which additional condition do leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs) have a potential role?
explanation: LTRAs such as montelukast can have a role in children with allergic rhinitis and may also be used in selected children with asthma, especially when inhaled therapy is difficult. They are not treatments for the other listed acute respiratory conditions.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Asthma Management: Medications and Devices - Part A

rationale: The original item was multiple-answer and listed several possible roles; to make it single-best-answer, it was rewritten to ask for one well-recognised additional paediatric indication.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. LTRAs can be used for allergic rhinitis in children.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Bacterial pneumonia is not an indication for LTRAs.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. Croup is treated with corticosteroids and sometimes nebulised adrenaline, not LTRAs.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Acute bronchiolitis is not treated with LTRAs.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Pulmonary oedema is not an indication for LTRAs.

Instructions

Question 7 - 9 relate to this case

Asthma Management: Medications and Devices - Case 3

David is a 2 year old boy with a history of frequent intermittent asthma. His asthma has been well controlled on fluticasone (Flixotide) 50 μg 1 puff BID (twice daily) and salbutamol (Ventolin). His cousin has been started on an ‘asthma pill’ and David’s mother wants to know if this is an option for David.
